I was a Los Angeles County Firefighter for 24 years going up through the ranks to Battalion Chief at the time I retired. I have led strike teams in major fires around the state and have been the incident commander on numerous brush fires. There is nothing unusual about the number of fires this year or even the location of some of them. It does break my heart to see the number of acres burned and the number of lives lost this year.

Some of the names of the current fires have been used over and over in the same general locations because numerous fires have started in the same general locations and burned over the same general area dozens of times in past years because of geographic features and wind patterns.

With red flag conditions of extremely low humidity and high hot winds, a fire can travel extremely fast, starting spot fires miles ahead of the main fire as embers and sparks are carried by the wind and dropped into tinder dry grass and debris. There have been times in the past when hundreds of fires are burning simultaneously throughout the state. Some larger fires depending upon the fuel load, and geographical features can generate their own weather patterns.

There are also numerous causes of fires during these hot, windy and dry conditions. I have seen fires started by a piece of broken glass acting like a magnifying glass and focusing the sun on a patch of dry grass. Downed power lines from high winds directly on the lines or felling trees and branches onto the lines. Heat from the catalytic converter in a vehicle driven over dry grass has started many, mower blades striking rocks and causing sparks, improper dousing of a camp fires, a carelessly discarded cigarette butt out the car window, and yes also arson.

I am making this comment simply to say that not everything is a conspiracy while at the same time in some cases poor "forest management/brush management", lack of fire and evacuation preplanning in populated risk areas and surveys of hazards as well as more and more movement of human habitation into hazardous brush and forest interfaces all increase the risk of high dollar and life risk in these areas.

As my heart cries out for the town and people of Pleasant Valley, I also remember a number of my fellow firefighters who lost their lives trying to protect people and property in the fires around California over the past years and the times that I feared for my own life fighting wind driven fires as they burned from the North West corner of the San Fernando Valley to the sands of the Pacific Ocean in a matter of hours.

I am not trying to shill or dampen the great investigative work and discussion on this site, just saying that not every fire is a conspiracy and that there are times when weather conditions in California and other places around the world that can make it nearly impossible to prevent fires from starting or to stop them spreading when they do.
